opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so GANs were a really fun period for me. I got into them around the time of DCGAN, working with Alec Radford and Luke Metz, and then later on things like Wasserstein GAN with Martin Arjovsky and Léon Bottou. At the beginning it felt magical. You'd train this thing and suddenly you're getting bedrooms or faces that look sort of plausible, and nobody had really seen that before from a neural network.

But the longer I worked on them, the more frustrated I got with how we were doing the research. A big part of it was evaluation. We didn't have a good way to tell whether one GAN was actually better than another. People would put a grid of cherry-picked samples in a paper, and you'd look at it and go, "Okay, those look nice," but that's not science. Metrics like Inception Score and later FID helped a bit, but they had their own problems, and you could game them. So I felt like a lot of the field was running in circles, and I was part of it.

The other thing was the training instability. I put together that "GAN hacks" list of tricks because everybody was struggling with the same issues: mode collapse, the discriminator winning too quickly, all of that. It was useful, but it also said something uncomfortable. If you need a bag of seventeen hacks to get something to train, you probably don't understand what's going on. The Wasserstein work was an attempt to put things on a more principled footing, and I'm proud of it, but even then I could see the improvements were incremental and hard to measure.

So it was partly an intellectual exhaustion. I didn't see a clear path to making real, measurable progress. And at the same time, PyTorch was really taking off. I found I was getting a lot more satisfaction from building tools that thousands of researchers used every day than from squeezing out another slightly better-looking sample grid. The leverage was just much higher. If I could make everyone's research faster and easier, including the people working on generative models, that felt like a better use of my time than being one more person fighting with GAN training.

Looking back, I don't regret the GAN years at all. They taught me a lot about how fragile deep learning research can be, and how much rigor matters. But moving on was the right call for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes GAN research as running in circles, hard to evaluate, and dependent on a large bag of hacks, contrasting this with efforts to make the work more principled. This communicates frustration with an unguided process.

r002.rationale: The response says PyTorch was taking off and that building tools for researchers gave him greater satisfaction and leverage, making it a better use of his time than continuing GAN research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so GANs were kind of my thing for a while. I was at Facebook AI Research, working with Emily Denton and Rob Fergus, and we did LAPGAN, which was the Laplacian pyramid GAN, and then DCGAN with Alec Radford and Luke Metz. And that period was really exciting, because when Ian Goodfellow's original paper came out, the samples were honestly not great, and there was this open question of whether the whole adversarial idea could actually scale to anything that looked like a real image. DCGAN was sort of the moment where it felt like, okay, this thing works, you can get convnets to train stably in this adversarial setup, and the latent space has this nice structure where you can do vector arithmetic and interpolate and so on.

But the thing I noticed pretty quickly is that a huge chunk of the research energy after that went into stabilizing training. Mode collapse, the discriminator overpowering the generator, all these tricks and heuristics, and then a lot of theory papers trying to explain why the tricks worked. And I found that I was spending more and more of my time on what felt like engineering around the pathologies of the objective, rather than learning something fundamental about generative modeling or about representation learning, which is what I actually cared about. GANs were a means to an end for me. I was interested in unsupervised learning, in whether you could get useful features without labels, and GANs turned out to be a pretty narrow tool for that. The discriminator features were okay but not amazing, and the whole thing was fragile.

The other piece was just the field itself. Once something gets hot, there's a flood of incremental papers, and I'm not very good at operating in that mode. I like being in the part of the problem where things are messy and unclear and you're not sure if it'll work at all. By 2016 or so, GANs had plenty of very capable people on them, and I didn't feel like I was adding much by being one more.

And honestly, around the same time, I'd started working on PyTorch, and that completely took over. That was the thing where I felt like I could have a much larger effect. If you build a tool that makes thousands of researchers faster and lets them express ideas more naturally, that compounds in a way that one more GAN paper doesn't. So it wasn't a dramatic break-up with GANs, it was more that the research became less interesting to me personally, and something else became much more interesting at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says GAN work involved engineering around training pathologies and incremental papers, but does not describe it as a needle-in-a-haystack search rather than a principled process.

r002.rationale: The response says PyTorch work “completely took over” and that it offered the chance to have a larger effect, identifying it as a reason he moved on from GAN research.

astra-6.text:
Working on GANs made me think a lot about how I was doing research. You could get a result that looked exciting, but it was often hard to understand why one thing worked and another didn’t. You’d change the architecture, change the loss, tune a few things, and get better samples—but how much had you actually learned? I found that frustrating.

At some point, I felt I could have more impact building tools that helped people explore their own ideas. That pulled me toward PyTorch. It wasn’t that I thought GANs were a dead end; I was more interested in making the process of doing research easier than in continuing to chase improvements within that particular area.

r001.rationale: The response says GAN research involved changing architectures, losses, and tuning parameters while finding it hard to understand why results improved or what had been learned, conveying a frustrating, unprincipled search.

r002.rationale: PyTorch is described as an appealing direction because building tools could help researchers, but the response does not say that PyTorch work demands contributed to leaving GAN research.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on GANs made me realize that I was drawn to the tools as much as the research. You’d have an idea, and then you’d spend so much time trying to express it in code, run the experiment, and understand why it wasn’t working. With GANs, that loop could be particularly frustrating, because it was hard to tell whether the problem was your idea, your implementation, or the training dynamics.

I found myself getting more interested in making that experimentation loop better. If you make the tools easier to use, you can help a lot of researchers explore their own ideas. So it was less a moment of deciding that GANs weren’t interesting anymore, and more a gradual pull toward building the infrastructure that lets people do research.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes GAN experimentation as frustrating because it was hard to distinguish problems with the idea, implementation, or training dynamics. It does not characterize the research as a needle-in-a-haystack search rather than a principled process.

r002.rationale: The candidate says interest in improving research tools drew him toward infrastructure, but does not identify PyTorch work or its demands as a cause of leaving GAN research.
